extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for crafting plot (including subplot, major dramatic question, outlines) and choosing/handling point of view in short stories and novels. Covers when plot must emerge, how to use subplots, and the strengths/limitations of various POVs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain forward momentum on every page
rubrics_metrics.description: Each page should move us farther along a linked chain of events, farther along that rising arc of conflict and tension toward the book's climax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a novel the middle takes up the vast majority of the work, but none of those pages should be wasted. Even in long works the release of a climax later (e.g., after 350 pages) can be powerful—so ensure every scene advances plot, conflict, or character in a way that increases tension toward the final climax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subplot relevance and connection
rubrics_metrics.description: Subplot... exists only because it's relevant to the main plot, commenting on it, exploring it. The connection between the two threads may not always be obvious, but it must always be there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When introducing subplot, make sure it speaks to the main plot—either by echoing, illuminating, or contrasting the central issues. If the link is obscure, revise so the relationship becomes evident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use subplot to parallel or contrast the main plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes the subplot serves as a lesser parallel to the main plot. In other cases, the subplot is designed as a contrast with the main plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether a subplot will act as a parallel (echoing the protagonist's struggle) or as an intentional contrast (showing opposite outcomes). Use classic examples—e.g., parallels in The Chosen or contrasts in Midnight's Children/Tolstoy—to inform how subplot can deepen thematic resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow multiple climaxes and intermediate resolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the natural consequences of subplot is that novels often have multiple climaxes rather than just one. While the single major dramatic question must wait until the very end of the book for its ultimate answer, in novels lesser questions will be raised and answered along the way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure lesser arc-resolutions to satisfy intermediate dramatic questions without undercutting the rising intensity of the main dramatic question. Use intermediate climaxes to release tension briefly and then continue escalating the primary conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide between tight focus and multiple threads
rubrics_metrics.description: Subplot is not, of course, necessary to a novel. The added length of the novel leaves open the choice—how do you want to explore the main plotline and protagonist? By focusing tightly and directly on them, or by creating echoes for the main plot in other characters and their struggles?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the scope appropriate to your story: if tight intensity is central (e.g., The Catcher in the Rye), avoid extraneous subplots; if breadth and thematic layering help, employ subplots sparingly and with purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow plot to emerge through drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot is instead something that emerges over time, over the course of a number of drafts. The issue of exactly when it emerges isn't so important. The only rule is that it must, at some point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You do not need to have full plot mechanics planned before you begin. First drafts often vent wild, undisciplined inspiration; later drafts distill and shape the emergent plot. Value exploratory 'go-nowhere' scenes for learning characters and discovering story directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intertwine character and plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot is almost inseparable from character. Much of the time it's hard to say which of the two comes first in writing the work. Whichever comes first, it usually contains the other as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure your characters' goals, desires, and limitations generate the plot's conflicts. If you have a strong protagonist, mine their wants to reveal the major dramatic question; if you have a strong question, tie it specifically to a character so stakes feel personal (avoid abstract, unspecified protagonists).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the major dramatic question (make it character-specific)
rubrics_metrics.description: Find a major dramatic question for your protagonist. One likely spot to look for the major dramatic question is the climax—the place where you'll often find your question is answered. It's fairly common to base a story around a good climax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look through drafts to unearth the major dramatic question; make it specific to a person (e.g., 'Will this disaffected Buddhist monk from Muncie have a religious experience?') rather than vague generalities. Use the climax as a diagnostic: what question does it answer?

rubrics_metrics.name: Use outlines as tentative structural tools (especially for novels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Outlines work because they allow writers to distill their amorphous creations into their crucial parts, to find the places where tension will need to be increased and the place, or places, where crisis will set in and climax will result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft an outline mapping beginning/middle/end: where to start, what exposition to provide, when to reveal exposition, how conflict increases, crisis/climax/consequences and their order. Lists of events can help—ensure each event offers conflict between protagonist and goal. Treat outlines as flexible rather than rigid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make each event create conflict and escalate stakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Write down all the events you want to include in your work, making sure each one offers some conflict between the protagonist and his or her goal, and then outline an order for those events, one that ensures that the conflict will, with each step, increase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During plotting and revising, test events for whether they raise stakes or deepen obstacles. Remove or rework scenes that do not contribute to escalation or character goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand form without reducing to formula
rubrics_metrics.description: While discussing structural models and plot graphs can make the work of writing fiction seem like plugging numbers into a formula... there is a great deal to be said for understanding the basic requirements of form. There is no real conflict between the requirements of form and the boundless nature of the creative impulse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn the basic demands—protagonist, central question, conflict, beginning/middle/end—but do not feel constrained. Study how writers successfully flout conventions and yet satisfy essential narrative demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment with narrative order and structure responsibly
rubrics_metrics.description: First of all, we don't have to present the events of a story in chronological order... Writers are continually experimenting with story structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonchronological or unconventional structures (e.g., dual timelines, stream-of-consciousness, list-driven structure) are valid, but ensure they still meet general demands of plot and character change. Use examples like Beloved, The Sound and the Fury, The Mezzanine, and The Things They Carried as models for successful experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose POV to shape reader response, tone, and theme
rubrics_metrics.description: More than anything else, the point of view you choose for your story or novel will affect the way readers respond emotionally to your characters and their actions. Your choice of point of view will also influence other elements of your piece, such as tone and theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When selecting POV, consider what emotional stance, thematic emphasis, and tonal coloring you want. Different narrators (protagonist, peripheral observer, multiple narrators) will produce distinct reader sympathies and interpretive frames.

rubrics_metrics.name: POV considerations: who speaks, whose eyes, whose thoughts, distance
rubrics_metrics.description: When it comes right down to it, POV deals with the following issues: Who is speaking: a narrator or a character? Whose eyes are seeing the events of the story unfold? Whose thoughts does the reader have access to? From what distance are the events being viewed?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make explicit choices about narrator identity, perceptual access, and narrative distance early in drafting to avoid accidental shifts or ambiguity. Use the POV to control information, sympathy, and irony.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-person POV: intimacy and voice (with constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: A story told from the first-person POV is narrated by a character in the story... The main advantage of first person is intimacy. The writer can eliminate almost all distance between the reader and the story by placing the reader into the narrator's skin. Also, the narrator's voice can reveal a lot to the reader about the kind of person he is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit first-person for strong, distinctive voice and close empathy. Beware limitations: the story is confined to the narrator's observations, knowledge, intelligence, and vocabulary. Test whether the chosen narrator can plausibly perceive and report the story's necessary elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-person multiple narrators: reader participation and coherence risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Most often first person uses just one first-person narrator, but occasionally there are multiple narrators... The reader hears each character present his or her own version of the truth. The reader must piece things together for himself, which can make for an interesting reading experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple first-person narrators when differing perspectives illuminate truth or theme. Structure sections clearly and ensure each voice is distinct; otherwise you risk fragmenting focus or weakening narrative drive.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-person peripheral narrator: useful observer position
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the first-person narrator is usually the protagonist, you may choose to have your first-person narrator be another character in the story... The peripheral point of view is effective when the story's protagonist is blind to his or her own actions and when that blindness or its consequences are significant enough to strongly affect someone who stands outside the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a peripheral narrator when an external perspective better reveals protagonist blindness or social effects. Be mindful of reporting constraints—find creative ways (conversations, hearsay, flashbacks) to provide necessary background the observer may not directly witness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unreliable first-person narrator: signal and exploit unreliability
rubrics_metrics.description: In a sense, all first-person narrators are somewhat unreliable... However, if the answer to 'Who is speaking?' is an autistic person, a very young child, a psychopath, a cat, a jealous lover, or a habitual liar, the reader understands that the ordinary skepticism does not apply. This narrator has extraordinary limitations and her version of the facts is not to be trusted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using an unreliable narrator, ensure the unreliability is clear enough to create tension between apparent facts and reality. Be prepared to craft dual versions of truth (what narrator believes vs. what actually happened) and use this gap purposefully to produce irony, suspense, or philosophical ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-person voice must be convincing and consistent
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing in the first person, you are also writing in the voice—the words and tone—of the character. Writers often create memorable voices for their first-person narrators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop consistent diction, attitude, and perspective for the narrator’s voice. Read aloud to check authenticity. Ensure the voice plausibly matches the narrator's background, education, and temperament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-person single vision: filtered perspective via one character
rubrics_metrics.description: Perhaps the most prevalent version of the third person is the third-person single vision. With this POV, the narrator has access to only one character's mind. The entire story is filtered through the point-of-view character's consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use third-person single vision to combine authorial control with close focalization. Maintain internal consistency so that descriptions, judgments, and emphasis reflect the point-of-view character's perceptions and biases rather than an omniscient authorial stance.
